summary:
Erzincan province stands under the Turkish national legal framework. No Erzincan-specific ordinance, incident or court decision was found on record, so what a trans visitor faces in the province is determined by national law and national policing practice.

The framework is contradictory on its face. Homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858, gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited by law. Those provisions coexist with the absence of any legal recognition for same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions or same-sex adoption, and with a bar on LGBTI people serving openly in the Turkish military.

The most direct threat to a visitor comes from the leaked 11th Judicial Package, an omnibus draft law reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. The draft would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", carrying penalties of up to three years' imprisonment. It would also sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by setting a minimum age of 25 and imposing onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges to be brought both against trans people and against the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification for the package is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The package is an omnibus vehicle that also carries unrelated measures, including longer sentences for children and provisions for online-content removal.

Public assembly by LGBT people is treated as an enforcement matter. Since 2015 Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. ILGA-Europe's press release of 7 December 2020 urged Turkish courts to acquit 19 human rights defenders prosecuted for taking part in a peaceful Pride march at Middle East Technical University in Ankara in May 2019, and called on the state to dismiss all charges and uphold its domestic and international commitments. The case establishes that even a campus Pride march can draw criminal prosecution, and the freedom-of-assembly climate it reflects is the framework under which a visitor in Erzincan would be judged.

In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Türkiye placed 7th from last, 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia. In early 2026 the government was reported to be considering going further, by criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality".
tangentialFactors:
The 11th Judicial Package is an omnibus legislative vehicle, and its LGBT provisions travel alongside measures on unrelated subjects such as child sentencing and online-content removal. The breadth of the package means the draft's fate is tied to wider legislative business rather than to LGBT policy alone.

Türkiye's position in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking, 47th of 49 with only Azerbaijan and Russia below it, places the country at the floor of a 49-jurisdiction European comparison set. The reported early 2026 consideration of criminalising public advocacy of conduct "contrary to biological sex and general morality" would extend exposure from status and healthcare into speech itself.

The pattern of prosecution for Pride participation predates the draft package by years: the Ankara campus march of May 2019 was still generating a public acquittal demand from an international LGBTI rights organisation in December 2020, indicating that assembly exposure is a standing feature of the legal environment rather than a new instrument.
localsOnly:
Same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption receive no legal recognition in Turkey, and LGBTI people are barred from serving openly in the military. These are resident-facing conditions of status that also shape how openly a person can live in Erzincan.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited by law, and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988. The gap between those statutory rights and enforcement practice is documented nationally: Pride marches have been banned and forcibly dispersed since 2015 with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions, and 19 human rights defenders were prosecuted for a peaceful campus Pride march in Ankara in May 2019.

For residents, the pending draft package carries the specific risk of criminal liability for gender-affirming healthcare, since it would expose both trans people and the professionals treating them to charges, alongside a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility conditions for that care.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Erzincan-specific ordinance, incident, arrest or court decision on LGBT or trans issues was found in the source inventory. The province-level picture is therefore unresolved rather than clear: absence of a recorded local case is not evidence that no enforcement action occurs there.

The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of the 29 October 2025 reporting and had not been passed at that point. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or abandoned is not sourced here.

The outcome of the prosecution of the 19 Pride march participants in Ankara is not stated in the sources; the December 2020 ILGA-Europe release is a demand for acquittal, not a reported judgment.

The reported early 2026 proposal to criminalise public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality" is described only as under consideration. Its legislative status and content remain unresolved.
